section.title: The God of All Comfort
section.sectionRationale: The most personal of Paul's letters opens not with rebuke or argument but with a doxology born of pain. Before defending his ministry, Paul blesses the God who had met him in crushing affliction in Asia, where he despaired even of life. He unfolds a theology of comfort: God comforts the afflicted so that they in turn can comfort others, and He teaches His servants to stop trusting themselves and to trust the God who raises the dead.
section.thesis: The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who meets His people in their deepest affliction, teaches them to rely not on themselves but on the God who raises the dead, and comforts them so that the comfort overflows to others.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the greeting to the church and the saints of Achaia; the blessing of the God of all comfort who comforts us so we can comfort others; and the deadly peril in Asia that taught Paul to trust the God who raises the dead, sustained by the prayers of the saints.

units.label: Greeting to the church
units.note: grace and peace from God our Father

verses.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God in Corinth, together with all the saints throughout Achaia:
Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.label: The God of all comfort
units.note: comforted so that we can comfort others

verses.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all {{paraklesis|comfort}},
who comforts us in all our {{thlipsis|troubles}}, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God.
For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows.
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which accomplishes in you patient endurance of the same sufferings we experience.
And our hope for you is sure, because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort.

units.label: Deliverance from deadly peril
units.note: we despaired of life, that we might trust the God who raises the dead

verses.text: We do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the hardships we encountered in the province of Asia. We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life.
Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who {{egeiro|raises the dead}}.
He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and He will deliver us. In Him we have placed our hope that He will yet again deliver us,
as you help us by your prayers. Then many will give thanks on our behalf for the favor shown us in answer to their prayers.

paraklesis.gloss: Comfort, consolation, encouragement, the strengthening that comes from one called alongside to help. The related verb parakaleo sounds through this passage like a refrain, appearing ten times in five verses. It is not a shallow soothing of feelings but the sturdy encouragement God supplies in the midst of trouble, the same word family used of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. Paul roots all such comfort in the character of God Himself, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort.

thlipsis.gloss: Pressure, affliction, tribulation, the crushing weight of hardship. The image is of being pressed or squeezed, as grapes under a press. Paul does not promise believers a life free of thlipsis; he promises the presence of God within it and comfort sufficient to bear it. The same afflictions that press the servant of Christ become the very occasion of God's consolation, which then overflows to others in their own troubles.

egeiro.gloss: To raise up, to awaken, to raise from the dead. It is the standard New Testament word for the resurrection of Jesus and of believers. When Paul says God raises the dead, he reaches for the deepest ground of hope available: the God who conquered the grave can be trusted in any peril, even when death itself seems certain. The lesson of Asia was to stop relying on self and to rely wholly on the God whose power is displayed supremely in resurrection.

basic.context: Paul opens his most personal letter with worship instead of argument. He had passed through an affliction in Asia so severe that he gave up hope of surviving. Out of that darkness he blesses God as the Father of all comfort, the One who comforts His people in their troubles so that they in turn can comfort others. The whole letter, a defense of true gospel ministry, begins from this well of consolation.
basic.hermeneutics: These verses are the doorway to the letter, setting its tone. Read the repeated word comfort as the theme: God comforts the afflicted, and that comfort is meant to flow onward to others. The account of the peril in Asia is not self pity but testimony, showing that even an apostle had to learn to stop trusting himself and to trust the God who raises the dead.
basic.originalLanguages: The keynote is paraklesis, comfort, with its verb sounding ten times in a few verses, the strengthening that comes from one called alongside. God comforts us in every thlipsis, every crushing affliction. And the lesson of Asia was to trust the God who raises the dead, egeiro, the resurrection word, so that hope rests on His power and not on our own.
basic.typology: The pattern of suffering that gives way to comfort, and of a death sentence answered by the God who raises the dead, mirrors the death and resurrection of Christ. As the sufferings of Christ overflow to His servants, so through Christ His comfort overflows, and the servant walks the road of the cross before the crown.
basic.christ: All comfort comes through Christ. God is named as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and it is the sufferings of Christ that overflow to Paul, and through Christ that comfort overflows in return. The God who raises the dead is the God who raised Jesus, so every consolation here is grounded in the resurrection of the Son.
basic.god: God is the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who does not stand aloof from His people's pain but meets them in it. He is sovereign even over deadly peril, delivering, and will deliver, and will yet again deliver. He is the God who raises the dead, and He is glorified as many give thanks for answered prayer.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 40 opens with God's command to comfort His people. Romans 8 promises that present sufferings are not worth comparing with the coming glory. Philippians 1 shows Paul again facing death yet full of hope. 1 Corinthians 15 grounds all hope in the resurrection.
basic.oneStory: The Bible is the story of a God who comes near to a suffering world. Here that God is named the Father of all comfort, who meets His servant in the valley of the shadow of death and teaches him to trust the God who raises the dead. The comfort received becomes comfort given, and the whole church is knit together in shared suffering, shared prayer, and shared consolation in Christ.

context.literary:
The opening of 2 Corinthians is carefully built, and its shape carries the message. Paul's usual letter opening has three parts: sender and address, a greeting, and a thanksgiving. Here the first two are standard, verses 1 and 2, but the thanksgiving is replaced by a blessing, 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ', verse 3. That is the form of Israel's own praise, a berakah, and it is the same form that opens Ephesians and 1 Peter. Paul usually says 'I thank God' for the people he is writing to. Here he blesses God for what God did for him, and only then turns to the Corinthians.

Verses 3 to 7 are a tight pattern of reciprocity in which a few words recur: comfort, affliction and suffering, and the little preposition 'for' that points outward, 'for your comfort'. The movement goes from God to Paul, from Paul to the Corinthians, and from the Corinthians' endurance back toward shared hope. Each clause balances the one before it, so the whole paragraph feels like a circuit through which consolation flows.

Verses 8 to 11 then change from teaching to testimony. The phrase 'We do not want you to be unaware' is a formula Paul uses to introduce news he thinks important, as in Romans 1:13 and 11:25. The story itself is vague, with no city, no cause and no date, because Paul's purpose is not to inform but to show what the affliction did. Verses 9 to 10 contain the climax of the passage, a short chain of purpose and result, 'in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead.' Verse 11 closes the circle by returning to the Corinthians: their prayers have a part in the rescue and will have a part in the thanks.

In the wider letter, this opening sets the key for the chapters ahead. The same pairing of suffering and comfort, of apparent weakness and God's power, comes back in 4:7 to 12 and 12:9 and 10.
context.historical:
Paul writes this letter within a year or so of 1 Corinthians, probably from Macedonia in the middle fifties of the first century, after a stressful stretch of dealings with Corinth. The relationship had been strained by a painful visit and a severe letter, 2:1 to 4, and by rivals who questioned Paul's credentials, 10:10 and 11:5. Titus brought good news about the Corinthians' response, 7:5 to 7, and the letter flows from that mixed relief.

The 'hardships we encountered in the province of Asia' are not described anywhere else in detail, and the church has long debated what they were. Paul says elsewhere that he had 'fought wild beasts at Ephesus', 1 Corinthians 15:32, that he faced 'many oppose me' there, 1 Corinthians 16:9, and that he was often near death, 2 Corinthians 11:23. Acts 19:23 to 41 records the uproar in Ephesus, and some think imprisonment or serious illness is in view. All we know is that the experience felt to him like a death sentence.

The Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey, was a place of intense pressure on early believers, from civic cults to the rivalry of trade guilds. Paul's churches there knew about it, and he writes 'brothers' in verse 8 to share it as family news.

The address is notable. The letter goes to 'the church of God in Corinth, together with all the saints throughout Achaia', verse 1. Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Cenchreae, the seaport of Corinth, as one of its congregations, Romans 16:1. The letter was meant to be read in a wider circle than one city, and this shaped how personal Paul could be.

Finally, the culture of the time prized strength and confident speech in public figures. Paul begins with an admission of near collapse, which in that setting was a startling way to open a letter that had to defend his apostleship.
context.canonical:
The language of comfort in these verses is rooted in the Old Testament. Isaiah 40:1 begins the second half of the book with 'Comfort, comfort My people', and the Greek translation uses the same word family that fills verses 3 to 7. Isaiah 66:13 gives the image of a mother's consolation, 'As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you', and Isaiah 51:3 promises that the LORD will comfort Zion and make her wasteland like Eden. The Psalms also anticipate the pattern, for example Psalm 23:4, 'Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me', and Psalm 94:19.

The phrase 'Father of compassion' draws on the great self revelation in Exodus 34:6, 'compassionate and gracious', and on Psalm 103:13, 'As a father has compassion on his children'. The Hebrew word for compassion is related to the word for womb, so it carries the feel of a parent's inward stirring.

The New Testament carries this theme forward. Simeon is waiting for 'the consolation of Israel', Luke 2:25, and Jesus says 'Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted', Matthew 5:4. John names the Holy Spirit as another Paraclete, John 14:16, from the same root as the comfort word, and 1 John 2:1 says we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous One. Paul himself writes that the God of endurance and encouragement gives unity, Romans 15:5, and that the Scriptures were written so that through endurance and encouragement we might have hope, Romans 15:4. The blessing of 1:3 is echoed almost word for word in Ephesians 1:3 and 1 Peter 1:3, and the end of the story, in Revelation 7:17 and 21:4, is God wiping away every tear.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Corinthians to see his suffering as a doorway to the gospel and not as a weakness that disqualifies him. This is the main thing he is doing in these verses, and it matters because some in Corinth were comparing him unfavorably with more impressive teachers. Instead of hiding the crisis in Asia, he tells it. He means them to notice that the same God who rescued him is now the source of their own comfort, and that his hardships were part of the way the gospel reached them.

He also wants them to see that suffering is shared. They have their own affliction, and Paul speaks of 'patient endurance of the same sufferings we experience', verse 6. In writing this way he binds himself to them and them to him, long before he has to say anything hard. The warmth of the opening is deliberate; it earns the right to speak plainly later in the letter.

A third aim is to establish the order of trust. The Corinthians had boasted of their own wisdom and strength, 1 Corinthians 4:8 to 10, and Paul shows from his own near death that trust in self is the thing God dismantles. His lesson is not 'be stronger' but 'learn where strength comes from'.

Finally, Paul invites partnership. Verse 11 gives the Corinthians an active part: they help by prayer, and when thanks rise 'from many', they share in the credit. He is not a lone hero but a man held up by the church.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage describes Paul's experience in Asia and it states a pattern of how God deals with suffering, but it does not promise that every believer will be rescued from every danger in the same way. Paul was delivered, and he expects further rescue, but elsewhere he accepts that rescue is not guaranteed in this life, Philippians 1:20 and 21, and that a thorn in the flesh can remain despite earnest prayer, 2 Corinthians 12:7 to 9. The sentence 'He has delivered us' is therefore testimony, not a formula.

What the passage does prescribe, in the sense of building a way of life, is the double movement of verse 4: receive comfort from God, and carry it to others in the same kind of trouble. The text is also clear that comfort is more than relief. It builds endurance, verse 6, and it places hope on a God who raises the dead, verse 9. Readers are meant to reflect on their own troubles in that light.

The text does not tell us to look for suffering or to hide struggles for the sake of appearing strong. Paul is open about despair, and he invites prayer. So the application is honesty about pain, dependence on God and a readiness to turn what we have received into comfort for someone else.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by 'the sufferings of Christ' that 'overflow to us' in verse 5?

views.label: The believer's own sufferings in union with Christ
views.case: Paul speaks elsewhere of 'the fellowship of His sufferings', Philippians 3:10, and of always carrying around 'the death of Jesus', 2 Corinthians 4:10. On this reading believers suffer because they belong to him, and their trials are shared with him.

views.label: Christ's own afflictions continuing in his body, the church
views.case: Colossians 1:24 speaks of filling up 'what is lacking in regard to Christ's afflictions for the sake of His body'. Here the sufferings of Paul as an apostle are seen as the way Christ's mission goes on in the world, so that what Paul endures is for others, as verse 6 says.

views.label: The final tribulation before the new age
views.case: Some take the phrase to draw on Jewish expectation of a period of suffering before the age to come, so that Paul describes himself as already living in the last days of affliction and consolation.

debates.bearing: The three views agree that the sufferings are joined to Christ and that comfort is joined to him as well, 'through Christ'. None of them says that Paul adds anything to the saving work of the cross. They differ on how closely the apostle's trouble is tied to Christ's mission.

debates.question: What was the affliction in Asia?

views.label: A violent attack or riot at Ephesus
views.case: Acts 19:23 to 41 and Paul's 'wild beasts' remark, 1 Corinthians 15:32, suggest a public threat to life. Paul's 'sentence of death' would fit an actual condemnation or mob danger.

views.label: A serious illness
views.case: The language of being under a burden 'beyond our ability' and despairing 'even of life' does not require human enemies. Some take it as a near fatal sickness, and note that 2 Corinthians 12:7 speaks of a bodily affliction.

views.label: Imprisonment or other legal danger
views.case: Paul says he had been in prison often, 2 Corinthians 11:23, and a stay in custody at Ephesus is held by some scholars, though Acts does not record one.

debates.bearing: Paul chose not to say, and the passage is built so that the unknown does not matter. The point is the response: despair, then a lesson to trust the God who raises the dead. The silence also lets any reader fit their own trouble into the pattern.

study.originalLanguages:
Several features of the Greek explain why this paragraph has such force. The first is the opening of the blessing. 'Blessed' is eulogetos, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the Hebrew berakah, as in Psalm 41:13 and Luke 1:68. In the Bible it is the word for praise addressed to God, not a wish for someone's good. The phrase translated 'Father of compassion' is, in the Greek, literally 'Father of mercies', a plural that comes from the Hebrew rachamim, whose root is the word for womb. It is not one act of mercy but all of them, an inexhaustible supply.

Second, the word for 'comfort' and its verb. They come from parakaleo, to call alongside, and carry a range: to console, to encourage, to urge and to appeal. The English 'comfort' leans toward softness, but the Greek word is the root of Paraclete, the name John gives to the Spirit and to Jesus, John 14:16 and 1 John 2:1. Comfort here is a presence that comes alongside and strengthens, not a pat on the head. It can also be translated 'encouragement' in several places, and the strongest reading holds the two together: help that restores courage.

Third, the verb for 'overflow' in verse 5, perisseuo, which means to be in excess, to abound. It is a favorite of this letter: Paul speaks of 'overflowing' joy, 8:2, grace, 4:15, and generosity, 9:8 and 9:12. The theme is that God's supply exceeds the demand. Suffering overflows, but comfort overflows more.

Fourth, the vocabulary of despair in verse 8. Paul says they 'despaired even of life', using exaporeomai, a strong compound of a verb meaning to be at a loss. In 4:8 he writes that believers are 'perplexed, but not in despair', and the two words there form a word play in Greek, aporoumenoi and exaporoumenoi, showing that Paul learned the difference in Asia: perplexity is allowed, total despair is not.

Fifth, the 'sentence of death' of verse 9 is apokrima, an official answer or verdict. And the perfect tense of the verb translated 'felt' tells us the verdict still stood in Paul's mind afterward. The purpose clause that follows is one of the sharpest in the letter, 'in order that we would not trust in ourselves'. The verb there is a perfect participle, 'having placed confidence', so the trust in self was a settled habit that God had to break.

Finally, the three tenses of rescue in verse 10. Paul says God 'has delivered us', 'will deliver us' and will 'yet again deliver us', a past, a future and a hope, all using the verb rhyomai, which is also the verb of 'deliver us from the evil one' in Matthew 6:13. At the end, in verse 11, thanks come 'from many faces', an idiom for many persons, and the verb for 'help' is a compound meaning to work together with, so that prayer is seen as labor shared.

typology.type: The sentence of death and the God who raises
typology.fulfillment: Abraham was told to offer Isaac, and the writer to the Hebrews says he reasoned that God could raise the dead, and 'in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death', Hebrews 11:19. Paul's sentence of death and rescue is another pattern in this line: a servant brought to the edge, and God's power shown in raising. In Christ the correspondence becomes literal. He alone died and rose, Romans 6:9. Paul's experience is only a shadow of that, so the type holds true in outline but is not an equivalent: Paul's rescue is a return to ordinary life, and Christ's is the beginning of the age to come.

Israel groaned in Egypt, and God said 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt', Exodus 3:7. Centuries later, Isaiah 40 opens with a command to comfort the exiles after judgment. Paul's paragraph repeats that shape: crushing trouble, then God's coming alongside. The escalation is that comfort is now through Christ and shared in the church, 2 Corinthians 1:5. The type falls short in that Israel's comfort was national and tied to land and return, while this one reaches wherever the believer is and is carried to others by individuals.

typology.type: The suffering servant and his helpers
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's servant is called to be 'a light for the nations', Isaiah 49:6, and Paul applies that commission to himself and Barnabas, Acts 13:47. The servant suffers for others, Isaiah 53:4 and 5, and Paul sees his affliction as 'for your comfort and salvation', 2 Corinthians 1:6. The correspondence is that a servant's pain becomes others' help. The climax is in Jesus, who bore griefs that no one else could carry, Matthew 8:17, and Paul never claims to do that. His sufferings serve the spread of the gospel, but only Christ's atone.

God led Israel in the wilderness to 'humble you and test you' so that they would learn that man does not live on bread alone, Deuteronomy 8:2 and 3. In Asia, Paul says, God broke his reliance on himself so that he would trust in God. The wilderness is a pattern of how God teaches dependence through emptiness. Jesus passes the same test, Matthew 4:4, where Israel failed, and so the pattern finds its fulfillment in him. The wilderness type falls short for believers because we pass the test only in union with him.

study.christ:
Christ appears in this paragraph at three points, and each one shows a different kind of connection. The first is in the very name of God. Paul blesses 'the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ'. He does not first say the God of Israel, though he surely means him, but defines God by his relation to Jesus. The God of all comfort is known as the Father of the Son, and the comfort Paul receives flows from that relationship. It means that the Old Testament God of compassion, Exodus 34:6, is the God who sent his Son, John 3:16.

The second is in verse 5, where Christ's sufferings 'overflow to us' and comfort overflows 'through Christ'. Whatever the exact meaning of the phrase, it ties the believer's trials to Christ's. Jesus told his disciples that they would have trouble, John 16:33, and told Saul that persecuting the church was persecuting him, Acts 9:4. The comfort is also through him, and Hebrews gives the reason: 'Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted', Hebrews 2:18. The Christ who comforts is the Christ who knows. He is a high priest who can sympathize with our weakness, Hebrews 4:15.

The third is the resurrection. 'God, who raises the dead' in verse 9 is not an abstract title. In 2 Corinthians 4:14 Paul states that 'the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus', and in Romans 4:24 that God 'raised Jesus our Lord from the dead'. The rescue Paul speaks of is an application of the resurrection power: God does for his servant, in small, what he did once for his Son in full. The pattern of the letter is that dying and living belong together, 4:10 to 12, and this paragraph introduces it.

There are also links of promise. Simeon waited for the consolation of Israel, Luke 2:25, and the child he held was that consolation. The Holy Spirit is a second Paraclete, John 14:16, so the one who comforts now is the Spirit of Christ, sent by him.

Care is needed. The paragraph does not say that Paul's hardship is the same as the passion, and it does not turn Asia into a staged crucifixion. It rests on what the New Testament explicitly says: that believers share in Christ's sufferings and in his comfort, and that the God who raised Jesus is the God who delivers his people. What Christ adds to Paul's comfort is not an example only but a presence and a promise that the last word over every death sentence is resurrection.
study.god:
This paragraph teaches that God is a comforter, and that comfort is something he is rather than something he sends. The titles in verse 3 are not decoration. 'Father of compassion' means that compassion belongs to God's very nature, in the way that a child's inheritance is his father's. 'God of all comfort' means that there is no kind of trouble that lies outside his consolation. Paul does not say that God occasionally comforts; the word 'all' is the thing.

He is also a God who allows affliction. The text does not pretend that the hardships were an accident or the work of an enemy alone. 'We felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves', verse 9. The 'in order that' says that God has a purpose in the trial. That does not make God the author of evil, and it does not explain every suffering. It says, in Paul's own case, that a sovereign God used a deadly crisis to teach a lesson that no easier circumstance could. The same pattern appears in Joseph's words, 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good', Genesis 50:20.

He is the God who rescues in time. The three tenses of verse 10 show a God whose faithfulness stretches across past, present and future. He rescued, he will rescue, and the hope that he will do so again is built on his record. Hope here is not wishful thinking but confidence formed by memory.

He is the God who raises the dead. This is the title that carries the whole passage. It does not say 'who can' but 'who raises', a continuous attribute. The sentence is bold for a Jewish believer: the God of Israel is the one who has power over the grave and has proved it in Jesus.

And he is a God who chooses to work through his people's prayers. Verse 11 is remarkable: the Corinthians' prayers help in the rescue. The text does not mean God needs help, but that he has chosen to bind himself to the prayers of his people, and that when answers come, the praise is shared. The doctrine of providence here is not a closed machine but a family conversation.

For worship, the paragraph shows a pattern in which praise comes first and explanation second. Paul blesses God before he tells the story, because the story is not a complaint but a testimony. A church learns from this that it can bless God in the middle of what it does not understand, and that its own pain, once comforted, becomes the means by which others are comforted.

crossReferences.note: The prophet's book turns from judgment to consolation with a command to speak tenderly to Jerusalem, 'Comfort, comfort My people'. Paul's use of the same word family places his own experience in that great movement: God who brings his people out of trouble and tells them to comfort one another.

God compares his own comfort to a mother's: 'As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you'. It adds a tender dimension to the 'Father of compassion' of 2 Corinthians 1:3, and shows that the compassion Paul invokes is parental rather than distant.

The LORD's self description, 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger', stands behind the 'Father of compassion'. Paul's blessing is a Christian version of Israel's confession: the same God, now revealed in the Father of Jesus, whose mercies are never exhausted.

The psalmist says that when anxious thoughts multiplied within him, God's consolations delighted his soul. It shows that an Old Testament believer knew the inward experience Paul speaks of in 2 Corinthians 1:4: comfort that arrives inside the trouble, not after it.

Paul holds that present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed, and that creation groans in labor pains. It gives the long view that 2 Corinthians 1 assumes, with the Spirit as firstfruits and hope as the reason believers wait.

Paul describes himself as hard pressed but not crushed, 'We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus'. It expands 1:5 and 1:9 and shows that the dying and living pattern of the first chapter governs the whole of Paul's ministry.

The thorn in the flesh and the answer 'My grace is sufficient for you' give a second case study of weakness that teaches dependence. Together with the Asia story it shows that the lesson of 1:9 is not a single event but a lasting principle.

Paul again faces possible death and writes with hope, relying on the prayers of the believers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. It is a parallel to 2 Corinthians 1:10 and 11, where prayer and rescue are joined and life and death are both gain.

Peter opens with the same blessing, 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ', and goes on to explain how trials prove faith. It confirms that this form of praise belonged to the common worship of the early church.

Jesus is a high priest who sympathizes with our weakness, and believers can approach his throne to receive mercy and grace in time of need. It supplies the Christ centered reason why the 'God of all comfort' of 2 Corinthians 1:3 actually understands the troubles of his people.

The ultimate comfort is shown as God spreading his tent over the multitude and wiping every tear from their eyes. It completes the movement that 2 Corinthians 1 begins: the God who comforts now will in the end remove the cause of the tears.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 explains why a letter like this needs to be written. The garden that was meant to be a place of rest became a place of toil and tears, and from then on, God's people knew affliction. Eve's pain and Adam's sweat belong to the same story as Paul's despair of life: a world broken at the root, in which even apostles feel crushed. The Bible answers not by denying the trouble but by showing how God meets his people in it.

The Old Testament moves toward the comfort that Paul names. Israel's sighing in Egypt is met by the God who sees and comes down, Exodus 3:7 and 8. Exile is met by the voice in Isaiah 40, and the promise to comfort Zion becomes the song of the second half of the book. The suffering servant is the one through whom the comfort arrives, Isaiah 53, and the comforter promised in Isaiah 61:1 to 3 is the anointed one who binds the brokenhearted and comforts all who mourn.

Christ is where those threads meet. He is the 'consolation of Israel', Luke 2:25, and he begins his ministry reading from Isaiah 61, Luke 4:18 and 19. He suffers, and in rising he becomes the source of a comfort that death cannot touch. The Spirit he sends is the Paraclete, John 14:16 and 26, who brings comfort into the hearts of believers, 2 Corinthians 1:22.

The church lives in this middle time. Paul is an example of how it works: believers are comforted, and they carry that comfort to others. The loop that verses 4 to 7 describe is the shape of church life, in which pain is not wasted because it equips someone to help another who is in the same kind of trouble. Prayer joins people across distance, verse 11, and thanksgiving rises from many.

And the story ends where the comfort is finished. Revelation 21:3 and 4 says God will dwell with his people, and 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes'. 'The former things have passed away.' The God of all comfort will no longer need to comfort, because there will be nothing left to grieve. Until then, every act of consolation, from a prayer to a visit, is a small piece of the age to come, brought forward by the God who raises the dead.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe God at the opening of the letter?

options.text: The Father of compassion and the God of all comfort.
options.note: Verse 3 names God precisely this way, setting the theme of the passage.

options.text: The God who keeps His people from all suffering.
options.note: God comforts in affliction; He does not promise a life free of it.

options.text: A distant judge who watches from afar.
options.note: Paul stresses God's nearness and compassion, not distance.

options.text: A God concerned only with Israel.
options.note: This comfort is for the whole church, Jew and Gentile alike in Christ.

quiz.q: Why does God comfort us in our troubles, according to verse 4?

options.text: So that we can comfort others with the comfort we ourselves received.
options.note: Comfort is given to be passed on to others in any trouble.

options.text: So that we will feel better and move on quickly.
options.note: God does bring relief, but the stated purpose is to equip us to comfort others.

options.text: So that we can prove we are stronger than our trials.
options.note: The point is reliance on God, not a display of our own strength.

options.text: So that we will never face trouble again.
options.note: Paul assumes ongoing affliction, met by ongoing comfort.

quiz.q: What did the deadly peril in Asia teach Paul?

options.text: Not to trust in himself, but in God who raises the dead.
options.note: Verse 9 states this as the very purpose of the ordeal.

options.text: To avoid dangerous places in the future.
options.note: The lesson was about trust in God, not merely caution.

options.text: That his own endurance was the key to survival.
options.note: The lesson was the opposite: to stop relying on himself.

options.text: That God had abandoned him in Asia.
options.note: God delivered him and would deliver again; He had not abandoned him.

quiz.q: What part did the Corinthians play in Paul's deliverance?

options.text: They helped him by their prayers, so that many gave thanks to God.
options.note: Verse 11 shows prayer as a real means God uses, leading to thanksgiving.

options.text: They sent money to fund his escape.
options.note: The text names prayer, not financial aid, as their help here.

options.text: They traveled to Asia to rescue him personally.
options.note: Their help was intercession from a distance, not a rescue mission.

options.text: They did nothing; deliverance was Paul's work alone.
options.note: Paul credits their prayers as part of God's deliverance.

questions: Paul blesses God as the Father of all comfort out of the depths of affliction. When you are pressed by trouble, do you turn first to worship of God, or to something else?
God comforts us so that we can comfort others. Who in your life is in trouble right now, and how might the comfort you have received from God flow through you to them?
The peril in Asia taught Paul to stop trusting himself and to trust the God who raises the dead. Where are you still relying on your own strength instead of on God?

Paul was honest with the Corinthians about despairing of life. Are you willing to be honest with fellow believers about your own struggles, so that they can pray and share the comfort of Christ with you?
The Corinthians helped Paul by their prayers. Whose deliverance might God be inviting you to share in through faithful intercession this week?

translationNotes.note: The words comfort and comforts translate the paraklesis word group, which appears ten times in these five verses; English cannot always show how insistently the theme is repeated in the Greek.
The province of Asia refers to the Roman province in what is now western Turkey, centered on Ephesus, not the continent of Asia.
The sentence of death renders a legal image of a death verdict; Paul felt as good as condemned, so that his hope had to rest entirely on the God who raises the dead.
